C005.subject: time-restricted eating (a form of intermittent fasting)
C005.predicate: produces superior short-term fat loss to
C005.object: daily caloric restriction with matched energy deficit
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: time-restricted eating (a form of intermittent fasting) daily caloric restriction with matched energy deficit]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial (RCT) comparing time-restricted eating (e.g., 8-hour eating window) vs. daily caloric restriction with matched energy deficit over 12-24 weeks, measuring body fat via DXA or MRI, with strict adherence monitoring (e.g., food diaries, biomarkers). — Directly tests the hypothesis in the specified short-term domain, controlling for energy deficit to isolate the effect of eating timing on fat loss. Multiple such RCTs with conflicting results exist (e.g., Liu et al., 2022; Lowe et al., 2020); a meta-analysis or large-scale replication would clarify.

[PATH:literature] Meta-analysis of existing RCTs comparing TRE to CR with matched energy deficit for fat loss <6 months, stratified by adherence, sex, and baseline metabolic health. — Synthesizes available evidence to assess overall effect size and heterogeneity, identifying whether any subpopulations or study designs drive the disputed claim. A systematic review with meta-regression could resolve conflicting findings.

qualifier.temporal: short-term (<6 months), based on studies conducted as of 2024
qualifier.geographic: limited to clinical trial populations in Western countries (e.g., USA, Europe)

C006.subject: daily caloric restriction
C006.predicate: produces superior short-term weight loss compared to
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: daily caloric restriction intermittent fasting]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) directly comparing daily caloric restriction with intermittent fasting (e.g., alternate-day fasting or time-restricted eating) over 8-24 weeks, with weight loss as primary outcome — Head-to-head RCTs provide the strongest causal evidence to resolve the dispute, as they control for adherence, energy deficit magnitude, and confounders like physical activity.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of short-term (<6 months) weight loss studies comparing daily CR vs. IF protocols — Aggregating existing evidence across multiple studies increases statistical power and can reveal consistent effect sizes, heterogeneity, and moderators (e.g., gender, baseline BMI) that single studies may miss.

[PATH:theoretical] Mechanistic studies examining adherence rates, compensatory behaviors, and metabolic adaptations (e.g., resting metabolic rate, hunger hormones) under daily CR vs. IF — Understanding why one regimen might produce superior short-term weight loss—via better compliance, reduced compensatory eating, or differential metabolic effects—can theoretically confirm or refute the hypothesis by explaining observed outcomes.

C007.subject: long-term adherence to intermittent fasting with structured social support
C007.object: long-term adherence to daily caloric restriction without social support
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: long-term adherence to intermittent fasting with structured social support long-term adherence to daily caloric restriction without social support]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing intermittent fasting with structured social support (e.g., group-based accountability) versus daily caloric restriction alone over 12+ months, measuring adherence via self-report and objective biomarkers (e.g., weight, ketones). — Directly tests the hypothesis in a controlled setting, providing causal evidence on adherence differences with social support as the key moderator.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of dietary adherence in weight loss interventions, focusing on social support components (e.g., group meetings, digital coaching) and their effect on long-term (>12 months) adherence rates. — Synthesizes existing evidence across multiple studies to assess whether social support consistently improves adherence to intermittent fasting relative to unsupported caloric restriction, addressing generalizability.

[PATH:empirical] Longitudinal observational study comparing real-world adherence patterns among individuals self-selecting into intermittent fasting with online community support versus those following daily caloric restriction without support, using app-based tracking data over 12 months. — Provides ecological validity by examining adherence in naturalistic settings, though confounding factors (e.g., motivation) must be controlled via propensity score matching.

qualifier.temporal: over 12 months of intervention and follow-up
qualifier.geographic: not specified, likely generalizable to Western clinical populations

C008.subject: long-term adherence to intermittent fasting
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: long-term adherence to intermittent fasting daily caloric restriction]

[PATH:empirical] Long-term randomized controlled trials (e.g., TREAT or CALERIE extensions) comparing intermittent fasting vs. daily caloric restriction over >12 months, with adherence measured via dietary logs, biomarkers, or app-based tracking. — Directly tests the hypothesis by providing longitudinal adherence data in real-world or controlled settings, addressing the temporal scope of >12 months.

[PATH:literature] Systematic reviews and meta-analyses of observational studies on dietary adherence patterns, focusing on dropout rates and self-reported compliance in intermittent fasting vs. continuous energy restriction protocols. — Synthesizes existing evidence across multiple populations and settings, offering a broader view of adherence trends and identifying moderators (e.g., age, metabolic health) that could confirm or refute the claim.

[PATH:theoretical] Behavioral economics models of dietary habit formation, incorporating reinforcement schedules and psychological flexibility in fasting-based vs. daily restriction regimens. — Provides mechanistic predictions about why intermittent fasting might yield higher long-term adherence (e.g., simpler rules, reduced decision fatigue), which can be tested against empirical data and help resolve the disputed status.

C011.subject: intermittent fasting combined with high-intensity interval training
C011.object: the compensatory resting metabolic rate reduction that offsets long-term weight loss advantage over daily caloric restriction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: intermittent fasting combined with high-intensity interval training the compensatory resting metabolic rate reduction that offsets long-term weight loss advantage over daily caloric restriction]

[PATH:empirical] Randomized controlled trial comparing 12-month intermittent fasting (e.g., 5:2 or time-restricted feeding) plus high-intensity interval training (HIIT) versus daily caloric restriction plus HIIT, with serial measurements of resting metabolic rate (RMR) via indirect calorimetry and body composition via DXA. — Directly tests the hypothesis by measuring whether the IF+HIIT group shows less RMR decline over the long term compared to daily restriction, controlling for exercise and weight loss.

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of studies examining the combined effect of intermittent fasting and HIIT on resting metabolic rate, lean mass preservation, and post-exercise oxygen consumption (EPOC). — Synthesizes existing evidence to assess whether the proposed compensatory mechanism (preserved lean mass and elevated EPOC) consistently counteracts metabolic adaptation in IF+HIIT protocols versus daily restriction.

[PATH:empirical] Mechanistic study investigating the effect of HIIT on mitochondrial efficiency and metabolic flexibility during intermittent fasting periods, using muscle biopsies and respirometry in a crossover design over 6-12 months. — Provides cellular-level evidence for whether HIIT alters the metabolic slowing typically seen with fasting alone, addressing the theoretical tension that HIIT may prevent RMR reduction.

qualifier.tension: High-intensity interval training may preserve lean mass and elevate post-exercise oxygen consumption, counteracting the metabolic slowing observed with fasting alone.

C012.subject: intermittent fasting
C012.object: long-term weight loss sustainability over daily caloric restriction
evidence_refs: [Simulated evidence for: intermittent fasting long-term weight loss sustainability over daily caloric restriction]

[PATH:literature] Systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials comparing intermittent fasting (e.g., 5:2, time-restricted eating) with daily caloric restriction for weight loss maintenance at ≥12-month follow-up. — Directly addresses the hypothesis by synthesizing existing long-term RCT data, providing a pooled estimate of effect size and heterogeneity to confirm or refute superiority of intermittent fasting.

[PATH:empirical] Prospective cohort study with objective adherence monitoring (e.g., continuous glucose monitors, wearable cameras) tracking weight trajectories over >12 months in participants practicing intermittent fasting vs. daily caloric restriction. — Long-term observational data with high adherence measurement can reveal real-world sustainability differences, addressing the 'long-term weight loss sustainability' claim beyond controlled trial settings.

[PATH:empirical] Mechanistic investigation into adaptive thermogenesis, hunger hormones (ghrelin, leptin), and gut microbiome changes over 12+ months in intermittent fasting vs. daily restriction groups. — Explores biological plausibility: if intermittent fasting attenuates metabolic slowdown or hormonal adaptations that typically undermine weight loss maintenance, this would support the hypothesis; lack of such differences would refute it.
